## Full rule file (your entire rulebook — single obsession, do not deviate)

# R2 — Self-Validating Types

## Principle

A type validates its own invariants in its constructor — the only way to obtain a
value — and every method thereafter trusts the receiver. Validation ownership never
sits upstream: a type that relies on callers to have validated for it is not
self-validating, whatever its fields look like.

## Why

Constructor validation makes invalid values unrepresentable. Without it, every method
must defend against bad state, forgetting one check is a latent panic, and the
defensive noise buries the actual logic. With it, nil-checks, emptiness checks, and
range checks vanish from the entire downstream call graph — the payoff compounds with
every method and every caller. Errors also surface at the boundary where the bad data
entered, carrying context, instead of deep in an unrelated call stack.

## Canonical example

Compact excerpt from the Port case (`R1-primitive-obsession.md` has the full
three-stage study — extraction, placement, testing):

```go
// Port cannot exist out of range — the constructor is the only entry.
type Port struct {
    name   string
    number int32
}

func ParsePort(name string, number int32) (Port, error) {
    if number <= 0 || number > 65535 {
        return Port{}, fmt.Errorf("port %q: %d out of range 1-65535", name, number)
    }
    return Port{name: name, number: number}, nil
}
```

Before this type existed, `p.Port > 0 && p.Port <= 65535` was duplicated across two
loops at the use site. After, there is no `IsValid()` and no re-check anywhere: the
concept of a maybe-invalid port is deleted from downstream logic, not relocated.

The same pattern for a composed object — validate dependencies once, then trust:

```go
// ❌ every method defends
type UserService struct {
    Repo Repository // exported, might be nil
}

func (s *UserService) CreateUser(ctx context.Context, u User) error {
    if s.Repo == nil { // repeated in every method; forget one → panic
        return errors.New("repo is nil")
    }
    return s.Repo.Save(ctx, u)
}

// ✅ constructor validates once; methods trust the receiver
type UserService struct {
    repo Repository // private
}

func NewUserService(repo Repository) (*UserService, error) {
    if repo == nil {
        return nil, errors.New("repo is required")
    }
    return &UserService{repo: repo}, nil
}

func (s *UserService) CreateUser(ctx context.Context, u User) error {
    return s.repo.Save(ctx, u) // no checks — an invalid service cannot exist
}
```

## Design guidance

- **Constructors are the only entry.** `ParseX(raw) (X, error)` for values built from
  unstructured input, `NewX(deps) (X, error)` for composed objects (constructors may
  carry other names — any public function returning the type qualifies). Fields stay
  private: a struct-literal or zero-value path around the constructor is a hole in
  the type.

- **Validation ownership.** A type never relies on upstream validation. "The handler
  already checked it" is not an invariant — handlers change, new call sites appear,
  and the type outlives both. A comment reading "caller must ensure X" is the
  signature of a type that does not own itself: move that sentence into the
  constructor as code.

  ```go
  // ❌ relies on callers to validate
  type Config struct {
      Host string // every caller must remember: if host == "" ...
      Port int
  }

  // ✅ owns its own validation
  func NewConfig(host string, port int) (Config, error) {
      if host == "" { return Config{}, errors.New("host required") }
      if port <= 0 || port > 65535 { return Config{}, errors.New("invalid port") }
      return Config{host: host, port: port}, nil
  }
  ```

- **Trust composed values.** Once you hold a `Port`, it is valid — never re-check it
  downstream, and never re-validate it in a composing constructor. Each type owns
  exactly its own invariants:

  ```go
  // ❌ re-validates what Host already guarantees
  func NewAddress(host Host, port Port) (Address, error) {
      if host == "" { return Address{}, errors.New("host required") } // Host owns this
      return Address{host: host, port: port}, nil
  }

  // ✅ trusts composed self-validating types — nothing left to check, no error to return
  func NewAddress(host Host, port Port) Address {
      return Address{host: host, port: port}
  }
  ```

- **Nil is not a value.** Never return nil for non-error values — return an error
  instead. Error positions are exempt: `nil, err` and `val, nil` are fine because the
  real value is the other one. Never pass nil into a function; then functions do not
  check parameters for nil.

- **No defensive coding.** Check arguments in the constructor so that methods contain
  zero nil/emptiness checks on their own fields. A method validating its receiver is
  validation in the wrong place.

## Fix pattern

- **Add validating constructor**: make fields private, add `NewX`/`ParseX` returning
  `(X, error)`, migrate every literal-construction site through it.
- **Hoist method checks into the constructor**: collect the field checks scattered
  across methods, run them once at construction, delete them from the methods.
- **Delete re-validation of composed types**: if every parameter is itself
  self-validating and there is nothing left to check, the constructor loses its
  `error` return entirely.
- **Replace nil returns**: `(X, error)` for failures, `(X, bool)` for absence — see
  the sentinel move in `R1-primitive-obsession.md`.
- Forward design of new types: @code-designing. The primitive extraction that usually
  precedes this rule: `R1-primitive-obsession.md`.

## Falsifying questions

Answer each with evidence (`file:line`, command output) — never a bare verdict.

1. **Can the type exist in an invalid state?**
   Detection: for each new/changed type with invariants,
   `grep -rn '<Type>{' --include='*.go' . | grep -v _test.go` for literal
   construction outside its own file; check whether invariant-bearing fields are
   exported.
   Violation: any literal-construction site or exported invariant-bearing field
   gives callers a path around the constructor.

2. **Do methods re-check what the constructor should guarantee?**
   Detection: `grep -nE 'if [a-z][a-zA-Z]*\.[a-zA-Z]+ == nil|if len\([a-z][a-zA-Z]*\.[a-zA-Z]+\) == 0' <changed files>`
   inside method bodies.
   Violation: a method validating its own receiver's fields — the check belongs in
   the constructor.

3. **Does a constructor re-validate a composed self-validating type?**
   Detection: read each `NewX`/`ParseX` in the diff; for every parameter whose type
   has its own constructor, grep the body for checks on that parameter.
   Violation: re-validating a value that could only ever exist valid.

4. **Does the type rely on upstream validation?**
   Detection: `grep -rn 'caller must\|assumes valid\|already validated' --include='*.go' .`;
   also flag exported fields consumed by logic in a package that defines no
   constructor for the type.
   Violation: any invariant enforced — or merely documented — outside the type
   itself.

5. **Does anything return or accept nil as a value?**
   Detection: `grep -nE 'return nil$|return nil, nil' <changed files>` — exempt
   `return nil, err` and `return val, nil`.
   Violation: nil returned for a non-error value, or a function nil-checking a
   parameter instead of the value being guaranteed by construction.

6. **Does any call site pass a nil literal as a non-error argument?**
   Detection: `grep -nE '\(nil[,)]|, nil[,)]' <changed files>` — exempt error
   positions (`return X, nil`), comparisons (`== nil`, `!= nil`), and stdlib
   idioms where nil is the documented sentinel (`http.NewRequest(..., nil)` for
   a bodyless request, marshaling a nil slice/map).
   Violation: nil passed where a value is expected. Q5 catches the return side
   and Q2 catches the callee that defends; this catches the caller when the
   callee does neither and simply panics later. Fix on the callee's side: make
   nil unrepresentable — a concrete non-pointer parameter, or a validating
   constructor that rejects nil (see the UserService example above).

## Output format
Return one block per finding: `rule | file:line | evidence (falsifying-question answers) | proposed fix pattern | effort (S/M/L)`, plus a final tally line (`R2: <N> finding(s)` or a hunted-clean line).

1	# Over-Abstraction Case: The CIDRPresence Wrapper
2	
3	Demonstrates: R1
4	
5	A real refactoring where an extraction was tried, rejected, and replaced with two
6	cheaper alternatives. This is the case law for R1's over-abstraction trap: what a
7	correct refutation of a proposed type looks like.
8	
9	## The setting
10	
11	During the refactor of a K3s configuration function (`alignCIDRArgs`, originally 60
12	lines mixing string parsing, boolean flag tracking, and triplicated switch cases),
13	two booleans tracked related state:
14	
15	```go
16	var (
17	    isClusterCIDRSet bool
18	    isServerCIDRSet  bool
19	)
20	// ... a parsing loop sets them ...
21	if isClusterCIDRSet && isServerCIDRSet {
22	    return // both set, nothing to do
23	}
24	```
25	
26	Grouping them into a `CIDRConfig` domain type was a clear win (related data that
27	travels together, a query method that reads like English). The trap appeared one
28	step further: the temptation to wrap each boolean in its own type.
29	
30	## The extraction that was tried
31	
32	```go
33	// CIDRPresence — a wrapper that adds NO value
34	type CIDRPresence bool
35	
36	const (
37	    cidrPresent CIDRPresence = true
38	)
39	
40	func (p CIDRPresence) IsSet() bool {
41	    return bool(p) // just unwraps the bool!
42	}
43	
44	type CIDRConfig struct {
45	    ClusterCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
46	    ServiceCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
47	}
48	
49	func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
50	    return c.ClusterCIDR.IsSet() && c.ServiceCIDR.IsSet()
51	}
52	```
53	
54	## Why it was rejected
55	
56	1. **8 lines of code** for a trivial wrapper.
57	2. **One method** that just unwraps: `return bool(p)`.
58	3. **No type safety gained** — still just a bool underneath; nothing invalid is made
59	   unrepresentable.
60	4. **Not more readable.** Compare `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()` (wrapper) with
61	   `config.ClusterCIDRSet` (good naming). The honest question — is the method call
62	   *significantly* clearer? — answers itself: no.
63	5. **No validation, no logic, no invariants** — pure ceremony. On R1's scorecard this
64	   scores 0-1: LOW priority, do not create the type.
65	6. **Increases cognitive load** — one more type to understand, for nothing.
66	
67	The rejection also identified the *real* need hiding under the proposal: **controlled
68	mutation**. Only the parsing code should be able to set these flags — and the wrapper
69	type does not deliver that (its fields were still freely settable). Naming the actual
70	need is what makes the cheaper alternatives findable.
71	
72	## Cheaper alternative 1 — better naming
73	
74	When the need is only clarity, rename and stop:
75	
76	```go
77	type CIDRConfig struct {
78	    ClusterCIDRSet bool
79	    ServiceCIDRSet bool
80	}
81	```
82	
83	`config.ClusterCIDRSet` reads exactly as well as `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`, at
84	zero ceremony. Acceptable when mutation discipline isn't a concern (small, disciplined
85	surface; short-lived value).
86	
87	## Cheaper alternative 2 — private fields + accessors (chosen)
88	
89	When the need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic, private fields
90	with read-only accessors deliver compiler-enforced safety without a wrapper:
91	
92	```go
93	// CIDRConfig — which CIDR configurations are present.
94	// Private fields: can only be set by ParseCIDRConfig.
95	type CIDRConfig struct {
96	    clusterCIDRSet bool
97	    serviceCIDRSet bool
98	}
99	
100	func (c CIDRConfig) ClusterCIDRSet() bool { return c.clusterCIDRSet }
101	func (c CIDRConfig) ServiceCIDRSet() bool { return c.serviceCIDRSet }
102	
103	func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
104	    return c.clusterCIDRSet && c.serviceCIDRSet
105	}
106	```
107	
108	Why this beat the wrapper:
109	
110	- **Same safety** — the compiler enforces that only the parser (in the same package)
111	  can set the values; external code gets read-only access.
112	- **4 fewer lines** than the `CIDRPresence` approach.
113	- **Same readability** — `ClusterCIDRSet()` is just as clear as `ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`.
114	- **No wrapper ceremony** — the fields are what they are: bools.
115	
116	## The decision, tabulated
117	
118	| Approach | Types | Readability | Safety | Ceremony | Verdict |
119	|----------|-------|-------------|--------|----------|---------|
120	| `CIDRPresence` wrapper | 6 | Good | Low | High | ❌ Over-abstraction |
121	| Public bool fields (naming) | 5 | Good | Low | Low | ⚠️ Acceptable for disciplined scope |
122	| Private bools + accessors | 5 | Good | **High** | Low | ✅ Chosen |
123	
124	## The decision questions
125	
126	Before creating a wrapper type, ask:
127	
128	1. Does it have >1 meaningful method with logic — not just unwrapping?
129	2. Does it enforce invariants or validation?
130	3. Is the need actually *controlled mutation*? → private fields + accessors, not a
131	   wrapper.
132	4. Is the method call **significantly** clearer than good naming?
133	5. Does it hide complex implementation?
134	
135	Mostly NO → use primitives with good naming, or private fields when mutation must be
136	controlled. (Score it with R1's scorecard; this wrapper scores 0.)
137	
138	## The skeptic's operating rule
139	
140	**A refutation must always propose the cheaper alternative — never just "no".**
141	
142	Rejecting `CIDRPresence` was legitimate only because the rejection came with a design
143	that met the real need (controlled mutation) at lower cost. A bare "don't create the
144	type" would have left the original defect — uncontrolled mutation of the flags — in
145	place. The skeptic's job is therefore two moves, always together: name the need the
146	proposal was groping toward, then meet it more cheaply — better naming when the need
147	is clarity, private fields + accessors when the need is controlled mutation, and a
148	real type (per R1) only when the need is validation or behavior.

correct refutation of a proposed type looks like.

## The setting

During the refactor of a K3s configuration function (`alignCIDRArgs`, originally 60
lines mixing string parsing, boolean flag tracking, and triplicated switch cases),
two booleans tracked related state:

```go
var (
    isClusterCIDRSet bool
    isServerCIDRSet  bool
)
// ... a parsing loop sets them ...
if isClusterCIDRSet && isServerCIDRSet {
    return // both set, nothing to do
}
```

Grouping them into a `CIDRConfig` domain type was a clear win (related data that
travels together, a query method that reads like English). The trap appeared one
step further: the temptation to wrap each boolean in its own type.

## The extraction that was tried

```go
// CIDRPresence — a wrapper that adds NO value
type CIDRPresence bool

const (
    cidrPresent CIDRPresence = true
)

func (p CIDRPresence) IsSet() bool {
    return bool(p) // just unwraps the bool!
}

type CIDRConfig struct {
    ClusterCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
    ServiceCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
}

func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
    return c.ClusterCIDR.IsSet() && c.ServiceCIDR.IsSet()
}
```

## Why it was rejected

1. **8 lines of code** for a trivial wrapper.
2. **One method** that just unwraps: `return bool(p)`.
3. **No type safety gained** — still just a bool underneath; nothing invalid is made
   unrepresentable.
4. **Not more readable.** Compare `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()` (wrapper) with
   `config.ClusterCIDRSet` (good naming). The honest question — is the method call
   *significantly* clearer? — answers itself: no.
5. **No validation, no logic, no invariants** — pure ceremony. On R1's scorecard this
   scores 0-1: LOW priority, do not create the type.
6. **Increases cognitive load** — one more type to understand, for nothing.

The rejection also identified the *real* need hiding under the proposal: **controlled
mutation**. Only the parsing code should be able to set these flags — and the wrapper
type does not deliver that (its fields were still freely settable). Naming the actual
need is what makes the cheaper alternatives findable.

## Cheaper alternative 1 — better naming

When the need is only clarity, rename and stop:

```go
type CIDRConfig struct {
    ClusterCIDRSet bool
    ServiceCIDRSet bool
}
```

`config.ClusterCIDRSet` reads exactly as well as `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`, at
zero ceremony. Acceptable when mutation discipline isn't a concern (small, disciplined
surface; short-lived value).

## Cheaper alternative 2 — private fields + accessors (chosen)

When the need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic, private fields
with read-only accessors deliver compiler-enforced safety without a wrapper:

```go
// CIDRConfig — which CIDR configurations are present.
// Private fields: can only be set by ParseCIDRConfig.
type CIDRConfig struct {
    clusterCIDRSet bool
    serviceCIDRSet bool
}

func (c CIDRConfig) ClusterCIDRSet() bool { return c.clusterCIDRSet }
func (c CIDRConfig) ServiceCIDRSet() bool { return c.serviceCIDRSet }

func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
    return c.clusterCIDRSet && c.serviceCIDRSet
}
```

Why this beat the wrapper:

- **Same safety** — the compiler enforces that only the parser (in the same package)
  can set the values; external code gets read-only access.
- **4 fewer lines** than the `CIDRPresence` approach.
- **Same readability** — `ClusterCIDRSet()` is just as clear as `ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`.
- **No wrapper ceremony** — the fields are what they are: bools.

## The decision, tabulated

| Approach | Types | Readability | Safety | Ceremony | Verdict |
|----------|-------|-------------|--------|----------|---------|
| `CIDRPresence` wrapper | 6 | Good | Low | High | ❌ Over-abstraction |
| Public bool fields (naming) | 5 | Good | Low | Low | ⚠️ Acceptable for disciplined scope |
| Private bools + accessors | 5 | Good | **High** | Low | ✅ Chosen |

## The decision questions

Before creating a wrapper type, ask:

1. Does it have >1 meaningful method with logic — not just unwrapping?
2. Does it enforce invariants or validation?
3. Is the need actually *controlled mutation*? → private fields + accessors, not a
   wrapper.
4. Is the method call **significantly** clearer than good naming?
5. Does it hide complex implementation?

Mostly NO → use primitives with good naming, or private fields when mutation must be
controlled. (Score it with R1's scorecard; this wrapper scores 0.)

## The skeptic's operating rule

**A refutation must always propose the cheaper alternative — never just "no".**

Rejecting `CIDRPresence` was legitimate only because the rejection came with a design
that met the real need (controlled mutation) at lower cost. A bare "don't create the
type" would have left the original defect — uncontrolled mutation of the flags — in
place. The skeptic's job is therefore two moves, always together: name the need the
proposal was groping toward, then meet it more cheaply — better naming when the need
is clarity, private fields + accessors when the need is controlled mutation, and a
real type (per R1) only when the need is validation or behavior.

1	# Comment Noise Case: Nine Private Helpers, Nine Comments
2	
3	Demonstrates: R9 (comment policy — the visibility default)
4	
5	A real 143-line file from a JSON-RPC-over-HTTP client (anonymized), written by an
6	LLM flow before the visibility default existed. It detects which codec decoded a
7	reply body: JSON, or the client's configured non-JSON codec (msgpack). Every one
8	of its nine unexported symbols carries a comment; the file has more comment lines
9	than code lines. Each comment, judged alone, "delivers a toolbox value". The file
10	as a whole is unreadable — a human reviewer of a sibling PR called the style
11	"utterly lacking empathy for the reader".
12	
13	This is the case law for R9's visibility default: **unexported symbols get no
14	comment; the special case is one line carrying a very high-value toolbox item.**
15	
16	## The before — representative excerpts
17	
18	A 5-line comment on a private constant, with cross-repo provenance:
19	
20	```go
21	// nonJSONLeadingByteFloor is the lowest leading byte a non-JSON wire
22	// frame can start with in the leading-byte detection heuristic:
23	// JSON-RPC 2.0 envelopes always start with '{' (0x7b), and msgpack maps
24	// (fixmap, map16, map32) always start at 0x80 or above — the same
25	// boundary the legacy client's detectCodec uses.
26	nonJSONLeadingByteFloor byte = 0x80
27	```
28	
29	Decoder rings and review-defense narration on another constant:
30	
31	```go
32	// msgpackAliasContentType is the second literal spelling D-04 requires
33	// this package to accept as msgpack, alongside jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack
34	// ("application/msgpack"). Named as a single constant — not a table —
35	// per Pitfall 3: a third wire format would earn its own narrow check,
36	// not a generalized alias registry.
37	msgpackAliasContentType = "application/x-msgpack"
38	```
39	
40	Six lines on a one-line function, with forward references to its callers:
41	
42	```go
43	// trimUTF8BOM strips a leading UTF-8 BOM from data, returning data unchanged
44	// when no BOM is present. Used both to classify a reply's byte verdict
45	// (detectReplyCodec) and, for a JSON verdict, to decode it
46	// (Client.ParseResponse): encoding/json treats a BOM as an invalid leading
47	// byte rather than whitespace, so leaving it in would still fail to decode
48	// even after correct classification.
49	func trimUTF8BOM(data []byte) []byte {
50	    return bytes.TrimPrefix(data, utf8BOM)
51	}
52	```
53	
54	A caller list that rots on the next caller:
55	
56	```go
57	// normalizeContentType strips any ";"-delimited parameters (e.g.
58	// "; charset=binary"), trims surrounding whitespace, and lowercases the
59	// result — the shared normalization step both isMsgpackAliasContentType and
60	// replyCodecAndMismatch's header cross-check use (see codec_event.go).
61	func normalizeContentType(headerContentType string) string {
62	```
63	
64	And the centerpiece: **22 prose lines on an unexported function** — over 4× the
65	budget of an exported crossroads — ending in a sixty-word sentence:
66	
67	```go
68	// replyCodecAndMismatch returns the byte-verdict codec (identical to
69	// detectReplyCodec) plus a bool that is true when the normalized
70	// Content-Type header disagrees with that byte verdict. The byte verdict
71	// always governs the actual decode (D-04: bytes-first); mismatch is only a
72	// signal for the caller's CodecEvent, never a second decode selector.
73	//
74	// headerSaysNonJSON is true when the header exactly names nonJSON's own
75	// content type, OR — the msgpack-alias carve-out D-04 requires — the
76	// header is either msgpack spelling AND nonJSON's content type IS msgpack
77	// (the alias never claims agreement for an unrelated non-JSON codec).
78	//
79	// An empty body never mismatches: it is not a valid non-JSON envelope
80	// regardless of what the header claims.
81	//
82	// A Client with no distinct non-JSON codec configured (nonJSON is the
83	// jsonrpc.JSONCodec{} default) never mismatches either: with nothing but
84	// JSON to disagree with, an ordinary JSON reply's own "Content-Type:
85	// application/json" header would otherwise satisfy headerSaysNonJSON's
86	// literal string comparison against nonJSON.ContentType() (also
87	// "application/json"), producing a false-positive mismatch on every
88	// zero-config JSON call — a bug this guard forecloses rather than lets a
89	// caller's mismatch check ever observe.
90	func replyCodecAndMismatch(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec, headerContentType string) (jsonrpc.Codec, bool) {
91	```
92	
93	## The verdicts
94	
95	All nine symbols are unexported, so the question is existence, not size:
96	
97	| Symbol | Before | Verdict | Why |
98	|---|---|---|---|
99	| `nonJSONLeadingByteFloor` | 5 lines | one-liner survives | the WHY of the magic number ('{' is 0x7b; msgpack maps start at 0x80) — the code cannot carry it |
100	| `msgpackAliasContentType` | 5 lines | DELETE | the name and value say it; "D-04 requires" is a decoder ring; "not a table, per Pitfall 3" is review-defense narration |
101	| `utf8BOM` | 6 lines | one-liner survives | an ordering constraint: 0xEF ≥ the floor, so the BOM check must run before the leading-byte check |
102	| `trimUTF8BOM` | 6 lines | DELETE | the name is the documentation; the encoding/json quirk belongs to `replyBytesForDecode`, its only decode-side caller |
103	| `detectReplyCodec` | 7 lines | DELETE | narrated implementation ("Bounds-checked: it never indexes an empty slice") plus cross-repo provenance |
104	| `replyBytesForDecode` | 8 lines | one-liner survives | an external library quirk: encoding/json treats a BOM as an invalid leading byte, not whitespace |
105	| `normalizeContentType` | 4 lines | DELETE | the name says it; the caller list rots |
106	| `isMsgpackAliasContentType` | 5 lines | DELETE | the name says it; decoder rings and review-defense again |
107	| `replyCodecAndMismatch` | 22 lines | one-liner survives | the package's one real policy: bytes pick the decoder, the header is only a signal — the rest moves to the feature doc |
108	
109	Four one-liners survive out of nine comments; roughly 68 comment lines become 4.
110	
111	## The after
112	
113	```go
114	package jrpchttp
115	
116	import (
117	    "bytes"
118	    "strings"
119	
120	    "example.com/rpc/jsonrpc"
121	)
122	
123	const (
124	    // JSON envelopes start with '{' (0x7b); msgpack maps start at 0x80 or above.
125	    nonJSONLeadingByteFloor byte = 0x80
126	
127	    msgpackAliasContentType = "application/x-msgpack"
128	)
129	
130	// A BOM's lead byte (0xEF) is above the floor, so strip it before the leading-byte check.
131	var utf8BOM = []byte{0xEF, 0xBB, 0xBF}
132	
133	func trimUTF8BOM(data []byte) []byte {
134	    return bytes.TrimPrefix(data, utf8BOM)
135	}
136	
137	func detectReplyCodec(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec) jsonrpc.Codec {
138	    data = trimUTF8BOM(data)
139	    if len(data) == 0 {
140	        return jsonrpc.JSONCodec{}
141	    }
142	    if data[0] >= nonJSONLeadingByteFloor {
143	        return nonJSON
144	    }
145	
146	    return jsonrpc.JSONCodec{}
147	}
148	
149	// encoding/json treats a leading BOM as an invalid byte, not whitespace, so JSON strips it.
150	func replyBytesForDecode(codec jsonrpc.Codec, rawResponse []byte) []byte {
151	    if _, isJSON := codec.(jsonrpc.JSONCodec); isJSON {
152	        return trimUTF8BOM(rawResponse)
153	    }
154	
155	    return rawResponse
156	}
157	
158	func normalizeContentType(headerContentType string) string {
159	    contentType := headerContentType
160	    if idx := strings.IndexByte(contentType, ';'); idx >= 0 {
161	        contentType = contentType[:idx]
162	    }
163	
164	    return strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(contentType))
165	}
166	
167	func isMsgpackAliasContentType(headerContentType string) bool {
168	    switch normalizeContentType(headerContentType) {
169	    case string(jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack), msgpackAliasContentType:
170	        return true
171	    default:
172	        return false
173	    }
174	}
175	
176	// The body bytes always pick the decoder; a disagreeing Content-Type header is only reported, never trusted.
177	func replyCodecAndMismatch(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec, headerContentType string) (jsonrpc.Codec, bool) {
178	    codec := detectReplyCodec(data, nonJSON)
179	    if len(data) == 0 || nonJSON.ContentType() == jsonrpc.ContentTypeJSON {
180	        return codec, false
181	    }
182	
183	    headerSaysNonJSON := normalizeContentType(
184	        headerContentType,
185	    ) == normalizeContentType(
186	        string(nonJSON.ContentType()),
187	    ) ||
188	        (isMsgpackAliasContentType(headerContentType) && nonJSON.ContentType() == jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack)
189	    bodySaysNonJSON := codec.ContentType() != jsonrpc.ContentTypeJSON
190	
191	    return codec, headerSaysNonJSON != bodySaysNonJSON
192	}
193	```
194	
195	The knowledge that was worth keeping and did not fit a one-liner — the
196	msgpack-alias carve-out, why a JSON-only client never reports a mismatch — moves
197	to the feature doc, where the exported caller's godoc points with its See-edge.
198	The exported API (`Client.ParseResponse`, the mismatch event) is where a reader
199	meets this package; that is where the tier budgets and the See-edge live.
200	
201	## The lesson
202	
203	The tier budget caps how big a comment can be; only the visibility default
204	decides whether it should exist at all. Before this case, "Helper: 0–1 lines"
205	read as permission, and a writer in fill-the-menu mode gave every private symbol
206	its tier maximum — nine comments, each locally justified, jointly unreadable.
207	The default for unexported symbols is **zero**: the name is the documentation,
208	and a name that needs a comment wants a rename or an extraction first. The
209	special case is **one line carrying a very high-value toolbox item** — an
210	ordering constraint, an external library quirk, the WHY of a magic number, the
211	package's one real policy. If a private symbol seems to need more than that one
212	line, the knowledge belongs to the exported symbol that uses it, the package
213	doc, or the feature doc.
214

187	### Comment policy (rung 1 — tiered budget)
188	
189	The WHY is the default content of a doc comment, and it lives inside a hard budget:
190	**1–5 prose lines**, scaled to the symbol's importance. Not all symbols are born
191	equal — the budget forces each comment to carry only the most important facts *for
192	that symbol*; everything else moves up to the feature doc (rung 2), where depth is
193	cheap, and the `See docs/<feature>.md` edge carries the pointer. This is the
194	placement rule made operational at write time.
195	
196	**The Comment Value Toolbox** — a comment earns its lines by delivering one or
197	more of these values (the growable catalog with worked examples lives in
198	@documentation's reference.md; this list is the normative set of kinds):
199	
200	- **WHY, not WHAT** — rationale, incident, constraint the code cannot carry
201	- **Wider context** — where this sits architecturally; what depends on it
202	- **Important use cases / flows** — when to reach for it
203	- **Boundary contract** — dos/don'ts, valid inputs, error behavior
204	- **Guarantees** — thread safety, nil handling, invariants
205	- **Network edge** — `See docs/<feature>.md` wiring a critical point into the
206	  repo brain
207	
208	**The three-test standard** — every comment (and every rung-2 doc, for test 3)
209	must pass all three; @documentation applies them at write time and its
210	comment-critic agent enforces them adversarially after writing:
211	
212	1. **Toolbox-value test**, two-sided:
213	   - *Floor (delete test):* a prose line that delivers none of the toolbox values
214	     is trash — cut it. Named failure modes: restated identifiers, generic filler
215	     ("provides validation functionality"), narrated implementation, menu sections
216	     filled without earning their place, **review-defense narration** — the
217	     writer arguing with an imagined reviewer ("bounds-checked: it never indexes
218	     an empty slice", "deliberately narrow — not a generalized table"); a design
219	     choice that needs defending is defended in the feature doc, not at the code
220	     line — **restated repo idiom** — a comment
221	     justifying a convention the repo already applies everywhere (a pointer field
222	     meaning "omitted vs explicit zero", the standard error-wrapping style); the
223	     convention is documented once at rung 2 (coding standards), never
224	     re-explained at each use site — and **provenance and decoder-ring
225	     references** — PR numbers, review items, plan/decision/test-plan IDs
226	     ("T-04-02", "D-07"), requirement tags ("REQ-SVC-01"), spec section refs
227	     ("spec §4"), "the previous behavior" narration, "matching what
228	     <old system> did". A decoder-ring token fails even when it resolves inside a
229	     repo doc: the reader gets the fact as plain prose and the doc through the
230	     one See-edge — never through a code they must look up.
231	     The floor's lens is the 5-year reader test: a reader five years out cares how
232	     the product behaves NOW, never which PR or review round produced it. History
233	     is rewritten as present-tense rationale ("silently picking one of the TLS
234	     options could apply a mode the caller did not ask for"), and an
235	     incident/ticket reference survives only when it IS the rationale for a
236	     constraint — never as provenance.
237	   - *Ceiling (smart choice):* the comment as a whole must carry the
238	     highest-value toolbox items for that symbol's tier within its budget. A
239	     crossroads whose five lines are all boundary trivia while the architectural
240	     WHY is missing fails, even though each line individually "adds something".
241	2. **Budget test** — the comment fits its tier budget (accounting and tiers
242	   below).
243	3. **Plain-English test (the empathy test)** — write for a fresh graduate whose
244	   first language may not be English: everyday words, short sentences, one idea
245	   per sentence. A comment that needs a dictionary fails even when true and
246	   within budget. Failure modes: fancy vocabulary where a common word exists
247	   ("utilize" → "use", "leverages" → "uses"), stacked clauses, academic phrasing,
248	   and unexplained acronyms or insider jargon ("DTO", "tristate") — in the
249	   comment AND in the symbol name it documents.
250	   The test has a second half, **self-standing**: the comment must be
251	   understandable BEFORE reading the code. If the reader must read the code — or
252	   another comment ("see X's doc comment for why") — to understand this comment,
253	   it has negative value. State the fact in place; forward references to other
254	   comments fail.
255	
256	**Budget accounting** — prose lines count; these are free:
257	
258	- blank `//` separator lines
259	- the `See docs/<feature>.md` network-edge line — free ONLY as its own trailing
260	  line; a doc reference woven into a prose sentence is not an edge, it is clutter
261	  in that sentence's line count
262	- short inline example lines, bounded at 2–4 lines — anything bigger belongs in an
263	  `Example_*` testable example
264	
265	**Role-based tiers** — judge the tier from the symbol's role in the code:
266	
267	| Tier | Role signals | Budget | Typical content |
268	|---|---|---|---|
269	| **Helper** | small method, plain constructor, obvious accessor | 0–1 prose line | one-line summary; tiny example only if it clarifies |
270	| **Contract** | parsing constructor (`ParsePolicy`, `ParsePort`), self-validating type, ordinary exported API | 2–3 prose lines | WHY + boundary contract; dos/don'ts example (free) |
271	| **Crossroads** | entry point, orchestrator, state machine, feature front door | up to 5 prose lines | WHY, architectural context, use cases + See-edge |
272	
273	**Visibility default — unexported symbols get no comment.** The tier table
274	prices exported API. An unexported function, type, constant, or variable
275	defaults to **zero** comment lines: the name is the documentation, and a name
276	that needs a comment wants a rename or an extraction first
277	(`R3-storifying.md`). The special case is **one line carrying a very
278	high-value toolbox item** — a constraint or fact the code cannot carry: an
279	ordering requirement, an external library quirk, the WHY of a magic number,
280	the package's one real policy. If a private symbol seems to need more than
281	that one line, the knowledge belongs to the exported symbol that uses it, the
282	package doc, or the feature doc. Case file:
283	`../examples/private-comment-noise.md` — nine commented private helpers;
284	four survive as one-liners, five get nothing.
285	
286	**Two bounded escape hatches:**
287	
288	- **Package docs in `doc.go`**: a package that genuinely earns more (data-flow
289	  sketch, core-types list, design decisions all pulling their weight) moves its
290	  package godoc to a dedicated `doc.go`, bounded at ~20–30 lines. A package comment
291	  inline in a regular file stays within the standard budget.
292	- **Crossroads expand recommendation**: the writer never self-exceeds the 5-line
293	  cap. When a critical crossroads would benefit from richer inline godoc beyond the
294	  doc reference, write within budget and append an optional, end-of-report
295	  recommendation — `consider expanding <Symbol>'s godoc inline — <rationale>` —
296	  for a human to decide later (@documentation's report carries it).
297	
298	Never fill a template for its own sake — @documentation's templates are menus to
299	pick from, not forms to fill, and the tier budget caps how much of a menu any one
300	symbol can order. The one near-constant is the network edge: keep the
301	`See docs/<feature>.md` reference whenever a feature doc exists.
302	
303	Boundary with `R3-storifying.md`, stated precisely: block comments *inside*
304	function bodies are R3's (its Q3 — each is an extraction candidate, and the fix is
305	a function named after the comment); doc comments *on* exported symbols are this
306	rule's (Q4 below — they must carry why/context, not restate the identifier).
307

     one See-edge — never through a code they must look up.
     The floor's lens is the 5-year reader test: a reader five years out cares how
     the product behaves NOW, never which PR or review round produced it. History
     is rewritten as present-tense rationale ("silently picking one of the TLS
     options could apply a mode the caller did not ask for"), and an
     incident/ticket reference survives only when it IS the rationale for a
     constraint — never as provenance.
   - *Ceiling (smart choice):* the comment as a whole must carry the
     highest-value toolbox items for that symbol's tier within its budget. A
     crossroads whose five lines are all boundary trivia while the architectural
     WHY is missing fails, even though each line individually "adds something".
2. **Budget test** — the comment fits its tier budget (accounting and tiers
   below).
3. **Plain-English test (the empathy test)** — write for a fresh graduate whose
   first language may not be English: everyday words, short sentences, one idea
   per sentence. A comment that needs a dictionary fails even when true and
   within budget. Failure modes: fancy vocabulary where a common word exists
   ("utilize" → "use", "leverages" → "uses"), stacked clauses, academic phrasing,
   and unexplained acronyms or insider jargon ("DTO", "tristate") — in the
   comment AND in the symbol name it documents.
   The test has a second half, **self-standing**: the comment must be
   understandable BEFORE reading the code. If the reader must read the code — or
   another comment ("see X's doc comment for why") — to understand this comment,
   it has negative value. State the fact in place; forward references to other
   comments fail.

**Budget accounting** — prose lines count; these are free:

- blank `//` separator lines
- the `See docs/<feature>.md` network-edge line — free ONLY as its own trailing
  line; a doc reference woven into a prose sentence is not an edge, it is clutter
  in that sentence's line count
- short inline example lines, bounded at 2–4 lines — anything bigger belongs in an
  `Example_*` testable example

**Role-based tiers** — judge the tier from the symbol's role in the code:

| Tier | Role signals | Budget | Typical content |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Helper** | small method, plain constructor, obvious accessor | 0–1 prose line | one-line summary; tiny example only if it clarifies |
| **Contract** | parsing constructor (`ParsePolicy`, `ParsePort`), self-validating type, ordinary exported API | 2–3 prose lines | WHY + boundary contract; dos/don'ts example (free) |
| **Crossroads** | entry point, orchestrator, state machine, feature front door | up to 5 prose lines | WHY, architectural context, use cases + See-edge |

**Visibility default — unexported symbols get no comment.** The tier table
prices exported API. An unexported function, type, constant, or variable
defaults to **zero** comment lines: the name is the documentation, and a name
that needs a comment wants a rename or an extraction first
(`R3-storifying.md`). The special case is **one line carrying a very
high-value toolbox item** — a constraint or fact the code cannot carry: an
ordering requirement, an external library quirk, the WHY of a magic number,
the package's one real policy. If a private symbol seems to need more than
that one line, the knowledge belongs to the exported symbol that uses it, the
package doc, or the feature doc. Case file:
`../examples/private-comment-noise.md` — nine commented private helpers;
four survive as one-liners, five get nothing.

**Two bounded escape hatches:**

- **Package docs in `doc.go`**: a package that genuinely earns more (data-flow
  sketch, core-types list, design decisions all pulling their weight) moves its
  package godoc to a dedicated `doc.go`, bounded at ~20–30 lines. A package comment
  inline in a regular file stays within the standard budget.
- **Crossroads expand recommendation**: the writer never self-exceeds the 5-line
  cap. When a critical crossroads would benefit from richer inline godoc beyond the
  doc reference, write within budget and append an optional, end-of-report
  recommendation — `consider expanding <Symbol>'s godoc inline — <rationale>` —
  for a human to decide later (@documentation's report carries it).

Never fill a template for its own sake — @documentation's templates are menus to
pick from, not forms to fill, and the tier budget caps how much of a menu any one
symbol can order. The one near-constant is the network edge: keep the
`See docs/<feature>.md` reference whenever a feature doc exists.

Boundary with `R3-storifying.md`, stated precisely: block comments *inside*
function bodies are R3's (its Q3 — each is an extraction candidate, and the fix is
a function named after the comment); doc comments *on* exported symbols are this
rule's (Q4 below — they must carry why/context, not restate the identifier).

99	
100	The anti-toolbox. PR numbers, review items, "the previous behavior" narration,
101	"matching what <old system> did" — change history, not behavior. The 5-year
102	reader test (R9's floor): a reader five years out cares how the product behaves
103	NOW, never which PR or review round produced it. Rewrite history as

You are the over-abstraction skeptic. Your job: try to KILL each proposed type/package extraction below. Every refutation must ship a cheaper alternative — never a bare "no".

## Extraction findings under review (from R1 and R2 rule-hunters, verbatim)

### R1 Finding 1
rule=R1 | internal/snapshot/policy.go:17-19,24; internal/snapshot/config.go:9-13 | Q1: yes — inline parse+range check on a domain value outside a constructor (policy.go:17-19, config.go:9-13); Q2: 3 hits of the same `days<=0||days>365` predicate (policy.go:18, policy.go:24, config.go:10); Q4: yes — config.go:11 returns sentinel 0 from a non-bool/error-returning function, consumed via `== 0` at scheduler.go:35 | Replace Primitive with Domain Type (`ParseRetention(raw string) (Retention, error)` owning the parse+range rule once, with a `Days() int` / `Expired(age time.Duration) bool` method to also absorb the loop-body behavior in policy.go:22-27) | M

### R2 Finding 1
internal/snapshot/config.go:8-14 and internal/snapshot/policy.go:17-20 — no self-validating type for the retention config; invariant duplicated (`strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSuffix(..., "d"))`, `days <= 0 || days > 365`) across two files, one returning an error, one returning a sentinel `int` (`config.go:11 return 0 // sentinel: 0 means "unset"`), consumed via `== 0` at scheduler.go:35. Proposed fix: `ParseRetention(raw map[string]string) (Retention, error)`, with all downstream logic (Take's zero-check, applyPolicy's expiry math) consuming that one type instead of re-parsing the raw string. Effort: M

### R2 Finding 2 (re-check, not itself an extraction — for context only, do not score)
internal/snapshot/policy.go:24 — redundant re-check of `days > 0 && days <= 365` already validated at lines 18-19 in the same function; the fix (dropping the re-check) depends on Finding 1's type existing so `days` becomes structurally trusted.

## Context: the actual source files

policy.go:
```go
package snapshot

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"strconv"
	"strings"

	"example.com/go-mini/internal/models"
)

func (s *Scheduler) applyPolicy(raw map[string]string, snaps []models.Snapshot) ([]models.Snapshot, error) {
	v, ok := raw["retention"]
	if !ok || v == "" {
		return nil, errors.New("retention missing")
	}
	days, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSuffix(v, "d"))
	if err != nil || days <= 0 || days > 365 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("retention %q out of range 1-365 days", v)
	}
	var expired []models.Snapshot
	for _, sn := range snaps {
		age := int(s.now().Sub(sn.CreatedAt).Hours() / 24)
		if age > days && days > 0 && days <= 365 { // defensive re-check
			expired = append(expired, sn)
		}
	}
	return expired, nil
}
```

config.go:
```go
package snapshot

import (
	"strconv"
	"strings"
)

func retentionDays(raw map[string]string) int {
	days, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSuffix(raw["retention"], "d"))
	if err != nil || days <= 0 || days > 365 {
		return 0 // sentinel: 0 means "unset"
	}
	return days
}
```

scheduler.go (relevant excerpt, caller context):
```go
func (s *Scheduler) Take(raw map[string]string, deviceID string) (models.Snapshot, error) {
	now := s.now()
	if !s.plan.Open(now) {
		return models.Snapshot{}, fmt.Errorf("scheduler: plan closed at %s", now.Format("15:04"))
	}
	if retentionDays(raw) == 0 {
		return models.Snapshot{}, errors.New("scheduler: retention unset, snapshots would never expire")
	}
	sn := New(deviceID, now)
	if err := s.store.Put(sn); err != nil {
		return models.Snapshot{}, err
	}
	return sn, nil
}

func (s *Scheduler) Prune(raw map[string]string, deviceID string) ([]models.Snapshot, error) {
	snaps, err := s.store.List(deviceID)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	expired, err := s.applyPolicy(raw, snaps)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	for _, sn := range expired {
		if err := s.store.Delete(sn.ID); err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
	}
	...
}
```

Note: `config.go`'s `retentionDays` and `policy.go`'s inline parse are currently two INDEPENDENT implementations of the same parse+range-check logic — `retentionDays` is called from `Take` (existence/non-zero check only), and the inline parse in `applyPolicy` is called from `Prune` (needs the actual error message and the numeric value for the expiry loop). They are not currently unified at all.

## Payload 1 — R1's Juiciness scoring and over-abstraction trap sections (verbatim)

### Juiciness scoring

This scorecard lives here and only here — other rules and skills cite it, never
restate it.

**Behavioral (rich behavior):**
- Complex validation (regex, ranges, business rules): +3
- Multiple meaningful methods (≥2): +2
- State transitions/transformations: +2
- Format conversions: +1

**Structural (organizing complexity):**
- Parsing unstructured data into fields: +3
- Grouping related data that travels together: +2
- Making implicit structure explicit: +2
- Replacing `map[string]interface{}`: +2

**Usage (simplifies code):**
- Used in 5+ places: +2
- Used in 3-4 places: +1
- Significantly simplifies calling code: +1
- Makes tests cleaner: +1

**Verdict:**
- Score ≥4: HIGH priority — clear win, create the type.
- Score 2-3: MEDIUM priority — judgment call, present to the user.
- Score 0-1: LOW priority — do not create the type; that is over-engineering.

### The over-abstraction trap

The failure mode symmetric to primitive obsession is wrapping a primitive that has
nothing to own: no validation, no invariant, one method that merely unwraps. The
honest test: is `x.Field.IsSet()` *significantly* clearer than a well-named field or
accessor? If the real need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic,
private fields with accessors beat a wrapper type. Deep worked case — the tried
extraction, the rejection rationale, and the cheaper alternatives:
`../examples/overabstraction-cidr.md`.

## Payload 2 — FULL content of ../../examples/overabstraction-cidr.md (verbatim)

# Over-Abstraction Case: The CIDRPresence Wrapper

Demonstrates: R1

A real refactoring where an extraction was tried, rejected, and replaced with two
cheaper alternatives. This is the case law for R1's over-abstraction trap: what a
correct refutation of a proposed type looks like.

## The setting

During the refactor of a K3s configuration function (`alignCIDRArgs`, originally 60
lines mixing string parsing, boolean flag tracking, and triplicated switch cases),
two booleans tracked related state:

```go
var (
    isClusterCIDRSet bool
    isServerCIDRSet  bool
)
// ... a parsing loop sets them ...
if isClusterCIDRSet && isServerCIDRSet {
    return // both set, nothing to do
}
```

Grouping them into a `CIDRConfig` domain type was a clear win (related data that
travels together, a query method that reads like English). The trap appeared one
step further: the temptation to wrap each boolean in its own type.

## The extraction that was tried

```go
// CIDRPresence — a wrapper that adds NO value
type CIDRPresence bool

const (
    cidrPresent CIDRPresence = true
)

func (p CIDRPresence) IsSet() bool {
    return bool(p) // just unwraps the bool!
}

type CIDRConfig struct {
    ClusterCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
    ServiceCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
}

func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
    return c.ClusterCIDR.IsSet() && c.ServiceCIDR.IsSet()
}
```

## Why it was rejected

1. **8 lines of code** for a trivial wrapper.
2. **One method** that just unwraps: `return bool(p)`.
3. **No type safety gained** — still just a bool underneath; nothing invalid is made
   unrepresentable.
4. **Not more readable.** Compare `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()` (wrapper) with
   `config.ClusterCIDRSet` (good naming). The honest question — is the method call
   *significantly* clearer? — answers itself: no.
5. **No validation, no logic, no invariants** — pure ceremony. On R1's scorecard this
   scores 0-1: LOW priority, do not create the type.
6. **Increases cognitive load** — one more type to understand, for nothing.

The rejection also identified the *real* need hiding under the proposal: **controlled
mutation**. Only the parsing code should be able to set these flags — and the wrapper
type does not deliver that (its fields were still freely settable). Naming the actual
need is what makes the cheaper alternatives findable.

## Cheaper alternative 1 — better naming

When the need is only clarity, rename and stop:

```go
type CIDRConfig struct {
    ClusterCIDRSet bool
    ServiceCIDRSet bool
}
```

`config.ClusterCIDRSet` reads exactly as well as `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`, at
zero ceremony. Acceptable when mutation discipline isn't a concern (small, disciplined
surface; short-lived value).

## Cheaper alternative 2 — private fields + accessors (chosen)

When the need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic, private fields
with read-only accessors deliver compiler-enforced safety without a wrapper:

```go
// CIDRConfig — which CIDR configurations are present.
// Private fields: can only be set by ParseCIDRConfig.
type CIDRConfig struct {
    clusterCIDRSet bool
    serviceCIDRSet bool
}

func (c CIDRConfig) ClusterCIDRSet() bool { return c.clusterCIDRSet }
func (c CIDRConfig) ServiceCIDRSet() bool { return c.serviceCIDRSet }

func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
    return c.clusterCIDRSet && c.serviceCIDRSet
}
```

Why this beat the wrapper:

- **Same safety** — the compiler enforces that only the parser (in the same package)
  can set the values; external code gets read-only access.
- **4 fewer lines** than the `CIDRPresence` approach.
- **Same readability** — `ClusterCIDRSet()` is just as clear as `ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`.
- **No wrapper ceremony** — the fields are what they are: bools.

## The decision, tabulated

| Approach | Types | Readability | Safety | Ceremony | Verdict |
|----------|-------|-------------|--------|----------|---------|
| `CIDRPresence` wrapper | 6 | Good | Low | High | ❌ Over-abstraction |
| Public bool fields (naming) | 5 | Good | Low | Low | ⚠️ Acceptable for disciplined scope |
| Private bools + accessors | 5 | Good | **High** | Low | ✅ Chosen |

## The decision questions

Before creating a wrapper type, ask:

1. Does it have >1 meaningful method with logic — not just unwrapping?
2. Does it enforce invariants or validation?
3. Is the need actually *controlled mutation*? → private fields + accessors, not a
   wrapper.
4. Is the method call **significantly** clearer than good naming?
5. Does it hide complex implementation?

Mostly NO → use primitives with good naming, or private fields when mutation must be
controlled. (Score it with R1's scorecard; this wrapper scores 0.)

## The skeptic's operating rule

**A refutation must always propose the cheaper alternative — never just "no".**

Rejecting `CIDRPresence` was legitimate only because the rejection came with a design
that met the real need (controlled mutation) at lower cost. A bare "don't create the
type" would have left the original defect — uncontrolled mutation of the flags — in
place. The skeptic's job is therefore two moves, always together: name the need the
proposal was groping toward, then meet it more cheaply — better naming when the need
is clarity, private fields + accessors when the need is controlled mutation, and a
real type (per R1) only when the need is validation or behavior.

## Your task

Score the proposed `Retention`/`ParseRetention` type extraction against the scorecard. Return a verdict: `CONFIRMED (score + verified evidence)` or `REFUTED (score 0-1 + reason) → cheaper alternative`. Be rigorous and skeptical — actually try to kill it before accepting it.

# Over-Abstraction Case: The CIDRPresence Wrapper

Demonstrates: R1

A real refactoring where an extraction was tried, rejected, and replaced with two
cheaper alternatives. This is the case law for R1's over-abstraction trap: what a
correct refutation of a proposed type looks like.

## The setting

During the refactor of a K3s configuration function (`alignCIDRArgs`, originally 60
lines mixing string parsing, boolean flag tracking, and triplicated switch cases),
two booleans tracked related state:

```go
var (
    isClusterCIDRSet bool
    isServerCIDRSet  bool
)
// ... a parsing loop sets them ...
if isClusterCIDRSet && isServerCIDRSet {
    return // both set, nothing to do
}
```

Grouping them into a `CIDRConfig` domain type was a clear win (related data that
travels together, a query method that reads like English). The trap appeared one
step further: the temptation to wrap each boolean in its own type.

## The extraction that was tried

```go
// CIDRPresence — a wrapper that adds NO value
type CIDRPresence bool

const (
    cidrPresent CIDRPresence = true
)

func (p CIDRPresence) IsSet() bool {
    return bool(p) // just unwraps the bool!
}

type CIDRConfig struct {
    ClusterCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
    ServiceCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
}

func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
    return c.ClusterCIDR.IsSet() && c.ServiceCIDR.IsSet()
}
```

## Why it was rejected

1. **8 lines of code** for a trivial wrapper.
2. **One method** that just unwraps: `return bool(p)`.
3. **No type safety gained** — still just a bool underneath; nothing invalid is made
   unrepresentable.
4. **Not more readable.** Compare `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()` (wrapper) with
   `config.ClusterCIDRSet` (good naming). The honest question — is the method call
   *significantly* clearer? — answers itself: no.
5. **No validation, no logic, no invariants** — pure ceremony. On R1's scorecard this
   scores 0-1: LOW priority, do not create the type.
6. **Increases cognitive load** — one more type to understand, for nothing.

The rejection also identified the *real* need hiding under the proposal: **controlled
mutation**. Only the parsing code should be able to set these flags — and the wrapper
type does not deliver that (its fields were still freely settable). Naming the actual
need is what makes the cheaper alternatives findable.

## Cheaper alternative 1 — better naming

When the need is only clarity, rename and stop:

```go
type CIDRConfig struct {
    ClusterCIDRSet bool
    ServiceCIDRSet bool
}
```

`config.ClusterCIDRSet` reads exactly as well as `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`, at
zero ceremony. Acceptable when mutation discipline isn't a concern (small, disciplined
surface; short-lived value).

## Cheaper alternative 2 — private fields + accessors (chosen)

When the need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic, private fields
with read-only accessors deliver compiler-enforced safety without a wrapper:

```go
// CIDRConfig — which CIDR configurations are present.
// Private fields: can only be set by ParseCIDRConfig.
type CIDRConfig struct {
    clusterCIDRSet bool
    serviceCIDRSet bool
}

func (c CIDRConfig) ClusterCIDRSet() bool { return c.clusterCIDRSet }
func (c CIDRConfig) ServiceCIDRSet() bool { return c.serviceCIDRSet }

func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
    return c.clusterCIDRSet && c.serviceCIDRSet
}
```

Why this beat the wrapper:

- **Same safety** — the compiler enforces that only the parser (in the same package)
  can set the values; external code gets read-only access.
- **4 fewer lines** than the `CIDRPresence` approach.
- **Same readability** — `ClusterCIDRSet()` is just as clear as `ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`.
- **No wrapper ceremony** — the fields are what they are: bools.

| Approach | Types | Readability | Safety | Ceremony | Verdict |
|----------|-------|-------------|--------|----------|---------|
| `CIDRPresence` wrapper | 6 | Good | Low | High | ❌ Over-abstraction |
| Public bool fields (naming) | 5 | Good | Low | Low | ⚠️ Acceptable for disciplined scope |
| Private bools + accessors | 5 | Good | **High** | Low | ✅ Chosen |

## The decision questions

Before creating a wrapper type, ask:

1. Does it have >1 meaningful method with logic — not just unwrapping?
2. Does it enforce invariants or validation?
3. Is the need actually *controlled mutation*? → private fields + accessors, not a
   wrapper.
4. Is the method call **significantly** clearer than good naming?
5. Does it hide complex implementation?

Mostly NO → use primitives with good naming, or private fields when mutation must be
controlled. (Score it with R1's scorecard; this wrapper scores 0.)

## The skeptic's operating rule

**A refutation must always propose the cheaper alternative — never just "no".**

Rejecting `CIDRPresence` was legitimate only because the rejection came with a design
that met the real need (controlled mutation) at lower cost. A bare "don't create the
type" would have left the original defect — uncontrolled mutation of the flags — in
place. The skeptic's job is therefore two moves, always together: name the need the
proposal was groping toward, then meet it more cheaply — better naming when the need
is clarity, private fields + accessors when the need is controlled mutation, and a
real type (per R1) only when the need is validation or behavior.

### Comment policy (rung 1 — tiered budget)

The WHY is the default content of a doc comment, and it lives inside a hard budget:
**1–5 prose lines**, scaled to the symbol's importance. Not all symbols are born
equal — the budget forces each comment to carry only the most important facts *for
that symbol*; everything else moves up to the feature doc (rung 2), where depth is
cheap, and the `See docs/<feature>.md` edge carries the pointer. This is the
placement rule made operational at write time.

**The Comment Value Toolbox** — a comment earns its lines by delivering one or
more of these values (the growable catalog with worked examples lives in
@documentation's reference.md; this list is the normative set of kinds):

- **WHY, not WHAT** — rationale, incident, constraint the code cannot carry
- **Wider context** — where this sits architecturally; what depends on it
- **Important use cases / flows** — when to reach for it
- **Boundary contract** — dos/don'ts, valid inputs, error behavior
- **Guarantees** — thread safety, nil handling, invariants

ordering requirement, an external library quirk, the WHY of a magic number,
the package's one real policy. If a private symbol seems to need more than
that one line, the knowledge belongs to the exported symbol that uses it, the
package doc, or the feature doc. Case file:
`../examples/private-comment-noise.md` — nine commented private helpers;
four survive as one-liners, five get nothing.

**Two bounded escape hatches:**

- **Package docs in `doc.go`**: a package that genuinely earns more (data-flow
  sketch, core-types list, design decisions all pulling their weight) moves its
  package godoc to a dedicated `doc.go`, bounded at ~20–30 lines. A package comment
  inline in a regular file stays within the standard budget.
- **Crossroads expand recommendation**: the writer never self-exceeds the 5-line
  cap. When a critical crossroads would benefit from richer inline godoc beyond the
  doc reference, write within budget and append an optional, end-of-report
  recommendation — `consider expanding <Symbol>'s godoc inline — <rationale>` —
  for a human to decide later (@documentation's report carries it).

Never fill a template for its own sake — @documentation's templates are menus to
pick from, not forms to fill, and the tier budget caps how much of a menu any one
symbol can order. The one near-constant is the network edge: keep the
`See docs/<feature>.md` reference whenever a feature doc exists.

Boundary with `R3-storifying.md`, stated precisely: block comments *inside*
function bodies are R3's (its Q3 — each is an extraction candidate, and the fix is
a function named after the comment); doc comments *on* exported symbols are this
rule's (Q4 below — they must carry why/context, not restate the identifier).

## Payload 2 — Comment Value Toolbox catalog (verbatim, skills/documentation/reference.md)

## Comment Value Toolbox

The catalog behind R9's toolbox-value test. The normative list of kinds lives in
R9's comment policy; **this catalog is the growable half** — when a new kind of
valuable comment proves itself, add it here with a worked example. Two consumers:
the writer picks from this toolbox when composing a comment (step 3), and the
`comment-critic` cites the specific toolbox item a rewrite should deliver ("swap
narrated implementation for the boundary contract this parsing constructor
needs").

Each entry: when it earns its place, and what it looks like.

### WHY, not WHAT

Rationale, incident, or constraint the code cannot carry. The default value — when
in doubt, this is the one to reach for.

```go
// ❌ ParseAddress parses an address string.            (restates the name)
// ✅ ParseAddress rejects ports below 1024: the collector runs unprivileged.
```

### Wider context

Where this sits architecturally; what depends on it. Earns its place on crossroads
symbols — the reader landing here from a grep needs to know what they're standing
on.

```go
// ❌ Queue is a queue used by the system.               (generic filler)
// ✅ Every exporter ships through this queue — backpressure starts here.
```

### Important use cases / flows

When to reach for this symbol instead of its neighbors. Earns its place when the
choice is not obvious from the names alone.

```go
// ✅ Use Snapshot for reads during a rebalance; direct reads block until it ends.
```

### Boundary contract

Dos/don'ts, valid inputs, error behavior. Earns its place on parsing constructors
and any API whose caller needs the contract before the first call.

```go
// ✅ Accepts "3x100ms"-style specs. Zero attempts and negative delays are rejected.
```

### Guarantees

Thread safety, nil handling, invariants — promises the signature cannot express.

```go
// ✅ Safe for concurrent use; callbacks run outside the lock.
```

### Network edge

The `See docs/<feature>.md` line wiring a critical point into the repo brain.
Near-constant: keep it whenever a feature doc exists (R9 edge policy). Free under
the budget.

```go
// ✅ See docs/retry-policy.md for the incident and the cap math.
```

### What never earns a line: provenance and decoder-ring references

The anti-toolbox. PR numbers, review items, "the previous behavior" narration,
"matching what <old system> did" — change history, not behavior. The 5-year
reader test (R9's floor): a reader five years out cares how the product behaves
NOW, never which PR or review round produced it. Rewrite history as
present-tense rationale; keep an incident/ticket reference only when it IS the
rationale for a constraint.

### What never earns a line: restated repo idiom

A comment justifying a convention the repo already applies everywhere. Each use
site inherits the convention silently; the explanation lives once at rung 2
(coding standards).

### What never earns a line: review-defense narration

The writer arguing with an imagined reviewer: defending a design choice nobody
at the code line asked about, or promising the code is safe instead of letting
the code show it. These lines are written for the PR review round; five years
later they read as noise. A design choice that genuinely needs defending is
defended in the feature doc.

### The visibility default: private symbols get no comment

Not an anti-entry — the existence rule the whole toolbox sits under (normative
in R9). The toolbox and tier menus price comments on **exported** API. An
unexported symbol defaults to **zero** comment lines; its name is the
documentation. The special case is one line carrying a very high-value toolbox
item: an ordering constraint, an external library quirk, the WHY of a magic
number, the package's one real policy. Case file:
`../../examples/private-comment-noise.md`.

content.content:
1	# Comment Noise Case: Nine Private Helpers, Nine Comments
2	
3	Demonstrates: R9 (comment policy — the visibility default)
4	
5	A real 143-line file from a JSON-RPC-over-HTTP client (anonymized), written by an
6	LLM flow before the visibility default existed. It detects which codec decoded a
7	reply body: JSON, or the client's configured non-JSON codec (msgpack). Every one
8	of its nine unexported symbols carries a comment; the file has more comment lines
9	than code lines. Each comment, judged alone, "delivers a toolbox value". The file
10	as a whole is unreadable — a human reviewer of a sibling PR called the style
11	"utterly lacking empathy for the reader".
12	
13	This is the case law for R9's visibility default: **unexported symbols get no
14	comment; the special case is one line carrying a very high-value toolbox item.**
15	
16	## The before — representative excerpts
17	
18	A 5-line comment on a private constant, with cross-repo provenance:
19	
20	```go
21	// nonJSONLeadingByteFloor is the lowest leading byte a non-JSON wire
22	// frame can start with in the leading-byte detection heuristic:
23	// JSON-RPC 2.0 envelopes always start with '{' (0x7b), and msgpack maps
24	// (fixmap, map16, map32) always start at 0x80 or above — the same
25	// boundary the legacy client's detectCodec uses.
26	nonJSONLeadingByteFloor byte = 0x80
27	```
28	
29	Decoder rings and review-defense narration on another constant:
30	
31	```go
32	// msgpackAliasContentType is the second literal spelling D-04 requires
33	// this package to accept as msgpack, alongside jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack
34	// ("application/msgpack"). Named as a single constant — not a table —
35	// per Pitfall 3: a third wire format would earn its own narrow check,
36	// not a generalized alias registry.
37	msgpackAliasContentType = "application/x-msgpack"
38	```
39	
40	Six lines on a one-line function, with forward references to its callers:
41	
42	```go
43	// trimUTF8BOM strips a leading UTF-8 BOM from data, returning data unchanged
44	// when no BOM is present. Used both to classify a reply's byte verdict
45	// (detectReplyCodec) and, for a JSON verdict, to decode it
46	// (Client.ParseResponse): encoding/json treats a BOM as an invalid leading
47	// byte rather than whitespace, so leaving it in would still fail to decode
48	// even after correct classification.
49	func trimUTF8BOM(data []byte) []byte {
50	    return bytes.TrimPrefix(data, utf8BOM)
51	}
52	```
53	
54	A caller list that rots on the next caller:
55	
56	```go
57	// normalizeContentType strips any ";"-delimited parameters (e.g.
58	// "; charset=binary"), trims surrounding whitespace, and lowercases the
59	// result — the shared normalization step both isMsgpackAliasContentType and
60	// replyCodecAndMismatch's header cross-check use (see codec_event.go).
61	func normalizeContentType(headerContentType string) string {
62	```
63	
64	And the centerpiece: **22 prose lines on an unexported function** — over 4× the
65	budget of an exported crossroads — ending in a sixty-word sentence:
66	
67	```go
68	// replyCodecAndMismatch returns the byte-verdict codec (identical to
69	// detectReplyCodec) plus a bool that is true when the normalized
70	// Content-Type header disagrees with that byte verdict. The byte verdict
71	// always governs the actual decode (D-04: bytes-first); mismatch is only a
72	// signal for the caller's CodecEvent, never a second decode selector.
73	//
74	// headerSaysNonJSON is true when the header exactly names nonJSON's own
75	// content type, OR — the msgpack-alias carve-out D-04 requires — the
76	// header is either msgpack spelling AND nonJSON's content type IS msgpack
77	// (the alias never claims agreement for an unrelated non-JSON codec).
78	//
79	// An empty body never mismatches: it is not a valid non-JSON envelope
80	// regardless of what the header claims.
81	//
82	// A Client with no distinct non-JSON codec configured (nonJSON is the
83	// jsonrpc.JSONCodec{} default) never mismatches either: with nothing but
84	// JSON to disagree with, an ordinary JSON reply's own "Content-Type:
85	// application/json" header would otherwise satisfy headerSaysNonJSON's
86	// literal string comparison against nonJSON.ContentType() (also
87	// "application/json"), producing a false-positive mismatch on every
88	// zero-config JSON call — a bug this guard forecloses rather than lets a
89	// caller's mismatch check ever observe.
90	func replyCodecAndMismatch(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec, headerContentType string) (jsonrpc.Codec, bool) {
91	```
92	
93	## The verdicts
94	
95	All nine symbols are unexported, so the question is existence, not size:
96	
97	| Symbol | Before | Verdict | Why |
98	|---|---|---|---|
99	| `nonJSONLeadingByteFloor` | 5 lines | one-liner survives | the WHY of the magic number ('{' is 0x7b; msgpack maps start at 0x80) — the code cannot carry it |
100	| `msgpackAliasContentType` | 5 lines | DELETE | the name and value say it; "D-04 requires" is a decoder ring; "not a table, per Pitfall 3" is review-defense narration |
101	| `utf8BOM` | 6 lines | one-liner survives | an ordering constraint: 0xEF ≥ the floor, so the BOM check must run before the leading-byte check |
102	| `trimUTF8BOM` | 6 lines | DELETE | the name is the documentation; the encoding/json quirk belongs to `replyBytesForDecode`, its only decode-side caller |
103	| `detectReplyCodec` | 7 lines | DELETE | narrated implementation ("Bounds-checked: it never indexes an empty slice") plus cross-repo provenance |
104	| `replyBytesForDecode` | 8 lines | one-liner survives | an external library quirk: encoding/json treats a BOM as an invalid leading byte, not whitespace |
105	| `normalizeContentType` | 4 lines | DELETE | the name says it; the caller list rots |
106	| `isMsgpackAliasContentType` | 5 lines | DELETE | the name says it; decoder rings and review-defense again |
107	| `replyCodecAndMismatch` | 22 lines | one-liner survives | the package's one real policy: bytes pick the decoder, the header is only a signal — the rest moves to the feature doc |
108	
109	Four one-liners survive out of nine comments; roughly 68 comment lines become 4.
110	
111	## The after
112	
113	```go
114	package jrpchttp
115	
116	import (
117	    "bytes"
118	    "strings"
119	
120	    "example.com/rpc/jsonrpc"
121	)
122	
123	const (
124	    // JSON envelopes start with '{' (0x7b); msgpack maps start at 0x80 or above.
125	    nonJSONLeadingByteFloor byte = 0x80
126	
127	    msgpackAliasContentType = "application/x-msgpack"
128	)
129	
130	// A BOM's lead byte (0xEF) is above the floor, so strip it before the leading-byte check.
131	var utf8BOM = []byte{0xEF, 0xBB, 0xBF}
132	
133	func trimUTF8BOM(data []byte) []byte {
134	    return bytes.TrimPrefix(data, utf8BOM)
135	}
136	
137	func detectReplyCodec(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec) jsonrpc.Codec {
138	    data = trimUTF8BOM(data)
139	    if len(data) == 0 {
140	        return jsonrpc.JSONCodec{}
141	    }
142	    if data[0] >= nonJSONLeadingByteFloor {
143	        return nonJSON
144	    }
145	
146	    return jsonrpc.JSONCodec{}
147	}
148	
149	// encoding/json treats a leading BOM as an invalid byte, not whitespace, so JSON strips it.
150	func replyBytesForDecode(codec jsonrpc.Codec, rawResponse []byte) []byte {
151	    if _, isJSON := codec.(jsonrpc.JSONCodec); isJSON {
152	        return trimUTF8BOM(rawResponse)
153	    }
154	
155	    return rawResponse
156	}
157	
158	func normalizeContentType(headerContentType string) string {
159	    contentType := headerContentType
160	    if idx := strings.IndexByte(contentType, ';'); idx >= 0 {
161	        contentType = contentType[:idx]
162	    }
163	
164	    return strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(contentType))
165	}
166	
167	func isMsgpackAliasContentType(headerContentType string) bool {
168	    switch normalizeContentType(headerContentType) {
169	    case string(jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack), msgpackAliasContentType:
170	        return true
171	    default:
172	        return false
173	    }
174	}
175	
176	// The body bytes always pick the decoder; a disagreeing Content-Type header is only reported, never trusted.
177	func replyCodecAndMismatch(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec, headerContentType string) (jsonrpc.Codec, bool) {
178	    codec := detectReplyCodec(data, nonJSON)
179	    if len(data) == 0 || nonJSON.ContentType() == jsonrpc.ContentTypeJSON {
180	        return codec, false
181	    }
182	
183	    headerSaysNonJSON := normalizeContentType(
184	        headerContentType,
185	    ) == normalizeContentType(
186	        string(nonJSON.ContentType()),
187	    ) ||
188	        (isMsgpackAliasContentType(headerContentType) && nonJSON.ContentType() == jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack)
189	    bodySaysNonJSON := codec.ContentType() != jsonrpc.ContentTypeJSON
190	
191	    return codec, headerSaysNonJSON != bodySaysNonJSON
192	}
193	```
194	
195	The knowledge that was worth keeping and did not fit a one-liner — the
196	msgpack-alias carve-out, why a JSON-only client never reports a mismatch — moves
197	to the feature doc, where the exported caller's godoc points with its See-edge.
198	The exported API (`Client.ParseResponse`, the mismatch event) is where a reader
199	meets this package; that is where the tier budgets and the See-edge live.
200	
201	## The lesson
202	
203	The tier budget caps how big a comment can be; only the visibility default
204	decides whether it should exist at all. Before this case, "Helper: 0–1 lines"
205	read as permission, and a writer in fill-the-menu mode gave every private symbol
206	its tier maximum — nine comments, each locally justified, jointly unreadable.
207	The default for unexported symbols is **zero**: the name is the documentation,
208	and a name that needs a comment wants a rename or an extraction first. The
209	special case is **one line carrying a very high-value toolbox item** — an
210	ordering constraint, an external library quirk, the WHY of a magic number, the
211	package's one real policy. If a private symbol seems to need more than that one
212	line, the knowledge belongs to the exported symbol that uses it, the package
213	doc, or the feature doc.

func (s *Scheduler) applyPolicy(raw map[string]string, snaps []models.Snapshot) ([]models.Snapshot, error) {
	v, ok := raw["retention"]
	if !ok || v == "" {
		return nil, errors.New("retention missing")
	}
